> Add embedded into has_feature might be a better solution to ensure consistency since it is similar to the feature tags like debugor editor?

I added "embedded" to `OS.has_feature` to returns true when the game is running embedded. I still kept `Engine.is_embedded` to be consistent with `Engine.is_editor_hint`. Sounds good?

> If multiple instances are configured, only the first instance will be embedded.
Is this a limitation? If not, you could embed multiple instances inside a TabContainer.

It's not a limitation, I was wandering if it's an actual good idea to have a couple of small game window inside the Game View. I built the `EmbeddedProcess` control specifically to be able to embed multiple processes easily. It's already a bit PR, I suggest it's done in another PR unless it's a priority?


> Also the WINDOW_FLAG_HIDDEN allows for making apps that minimize to tray I think? (we already support tray icons)

The `WINDOW_FLAG_HIDDEN` flag was added to be able to start a process completely invisible but still running at the desired size. It's important if you start the game and the `Focus the Game View when the project runs` options is turned off and you are not in the `Game` tab. Otherwise, the game window should be displayed over the editor.

> I don't know how, but I'm able to resize the window out of bounds in my game

The modification of the size and the position was not blocked when embedded. I added validations to block those, it should fix the issue.

> Editor becomes black when game starts in fullscreen

I was not able to reproduce by just setting `Fullscreen` in `Project settings > Display > Window > Mode`. I'll need more information or an MRP to figure out that settings is changed when your game starts.

> When you close game and the editor automatically moves focus to Script tab, the caret is invisible

Another fight with Windows. When the embedded process stops and it was focused, Windows does not reactive correctly the parent window. I forced the parent window to refocus/reactivate when an embedded window is closed on Windows.

> When you record the editor (tested with Game Bar recorder (Windows+Alt+R), but probably applies to OBS too), the running project is not visible in the recording. Probably expected though.

Yeah, that's to be expected and not much I could do about it. I guess because it's 2 different processes. I tested with OBS when capturing the hole screen or a screen region and it's working. I added a known issue in the PR description.

I feel like exposing `is_embedded` or similar to scripts is unnecessary. It feels like future-proofing with no demand. I'd wait for it to be requested first.

> > Add embedded into has_feature might be a better solution to ensure consistency since it is similar to the feature tags like debugor editor?
> 
> I added "embedded" to `OS.has_feature` to returns true when the game is running embedded. I still kept `Engine.is_embedded` to be consistent with `Engine.is_editor_hint`. Sounds good?

The reply suggested `embedded` should be a [feature tag](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/tutorials/export/feature_tags.html), like `debug`, `web`, `editor`, etc. This would also allow project settings overrides for embedded builds.
If we really need to expose a method, putting it in OS is also entirely arbitrary. I would not recommend it. The closest thing would be `OS.is_debug_build()`. However, `embedded` is currently not a feature tag, yet `debug` is and it corresponds to `OS.is_debug_build()`. So it makes even less sense.

Here's an issue that I've discovered that I don't think has been mentioned yet:

Godot v4.4.dev (833737aa3) - Windows 10.0.19045 - Multi-window, 1 monitor - Vulkan (Forward+) - dedicated NVIDIA GeForce GTX 980 Ti (NVIDIA; 32.0.15.6603) - Intel(R) Core(TM) i7-6700K CPU @ 4.00GHz (8 threads)

1. In the Script workspace, click "Make the script editor floating."
2. Run the game as embedded
3. With the Game workspace active, click the Script workspace button
4. **Bug:** The Script editor window is not brought to the forefront.

If you instead clicked the Script editor when the 2D/3D workspaces are active, this issue does not happen and the Script editor window is correctly brought to the forefront.

I expect that I would not use this embedded mode very often because it prevents me from being able to use the 2D/3D workspaces while also interacting with my game at the same time.

_But..._ if the embedded mode could be made floating, the same as the Script editor, I would use the embedded mode all of the time! In fact, I would prefer this to be the default behaviour in Godot. Here's what it would look like with embedded mode enabled and the Game workspace made "floating":

**Embed the game process within the editor: On/Off:** This button would be removed entirely from the Game workspace and moved to Editor Settings. (Default: Enabled)

**Make the Game workspace floating:** This new button would match the existing Script editor feature. (Default: Disabled??)

![floating-mode-button](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/80004f93-18a3-411e-99cc-538a07b704f6)

Once the Game workspace has been made floating, it would behave similar to the floating Script editor, except that it could be changed to not floating by using a button instead of closing the window. Closing the window would stop playback and change back to not-floating mode.

![embedding2](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/567bd3e5-e8dd-4669-9be1-b4c88bc759f6)

Alternatively, this could behave exactly like the Script window and there would be no button to move the Game workspace back to not floating. Instead, closing the window would simply change it back to not floating and the game would continue running.

If it is not possible to change floating/not floating mode while the game is running, I think that's entirely OK! **The important part is being able to use the Game workspace at the same time that you're able to use the 2D/3D workspaces.**
I'm also in favor of making the "window floating" button to be toggle-on instead of toggle-off, as the embedding is going to be the default. But I don't see a need for it to be in the right side.

While I think a lot of the frontend stuff for this seems pretty solid, I still don't know if this is fully implemented in the preferred way. Under the hood, its still treated as a seperate window, meaning this feature still does not play nice with application screen capture software. Neither Discord or OBS can capture both the editor with the embedded game window as a result. I think what I was hoping for is we would figure out how to get the game window to share the viewport texture with the editor at a much lower level (cross-application Vulkan handles https://registry.khronos.org/vulkan/specs/1.1-extensions/html/vkspec.html#VK_KHR_external_memory_fd).

I also notice that using the Windows command to switch windows between screens (Shift+Windows+Left/Right Arrow) makes the embedded window break outside of the editor's frame.

I think this is really cool and a step in the right direction, and I'd be happy to move forward with this, but I also hope we can figure out how to extend this to allow more lower-level embedding where its supported.

> I'm also in favor of making the "window floating" button to be toggle-on instead of toggle-off, as the embedding is going to be the default. But I don't see a need for it to be in the right side.

Ah, I see what you mean. In this case, embedding would be on by default (can be turned off in editor settings) and floating Game workspace would also be on by default (and can be changed to be not-floating with the tap of this toggle button). In this case, you could argue that this is _not_ the same behaviour as the floating window mode of the Script editor, and thus should not have the same GUI.

In my original post, I did start out by expressing a preference for floating mode to be enabled by default, but the rest of my proposal was actually designed to follow more closely with the Script editor behaviour, where floating mode is disabled by default. In this case, where floating mode is disabled by default for the Game workspace, the floating mode behaviour would be identical Script editor and the GUI for it should therefore be identical, with the floating mode button on the right side, sharing the same icon as the Script editor.

My preferences aren't extremely strong on this one. I can see advantages to either default:

**Floating mode enabled by default:** Simply builds on the existing Godot workflow of having the game window separate from the editor, which allows you to see your game and the other workspaces at the same time. This is a notable improvement over the existing Godot workflow because it adds all the benefits of the new Game workspace (the top bar with selection controls, etc.) to the separate game window (possibly a "best of both worlds" for most users??). Not sure about what happens when the game stops, though. Does this close the floating window entirely and move it back to the main editor? Or does the Game workspace remain floating in its position? This idea might need some actual user-testing of the implementation details.

**Floating mode off by default**: Follows the existing Script workspace GUI behaviour. The Game workspace can be left in a floating window when the game stops, resized to the user's preference, and the game will always launch in this floating window. I saw this as a "safer" option in terms of implementation details, simply because this idea of a floating workspace has already been implemented entirely with the Script editor.

Following suggestions from @allenwp and @YeldhamDev, I experimented with creating a floating window option for the Game View.

### Note: This is a work-in-progress prototype, intended to gather feedback.

#### Changes Made:
- **Toolbar Menu**: Added a toolbar menu with the following options (all enabled by default):
  - **Embed Game on Play**: Toggles embedding of the Game View.
  - **Float Game View on Play**: If the Game View is not already floating when the game starts, it will open in a floating window.
  - **Close Game View on Stop**: Automatically closes the Game View when the game stops.

- **Default Behavior**: These settings mimic the current Godot workflow, with the addition of a new Game View toolbar.

- **Enhanced Flexibility**: This setup provides users with added control over the Game View experience, potentially offering more flexibility than needed.

- **Manual Floating Option**: Added a "Make Floating" option, allowing users to open the Game View in a floating window and move it around without starting the game.

- **Unfocused Start Option Removed**: Removed the option to start the game "unfocused," as it required additional functionality in Windows to work with a new window.

I believe I understand this perspective: The whole reason for a floating window is to give access to the embedded Game workspace separate from the other workspaces.

...But when I think through why a user might disable embedded mode, it reveals a good use case to allow the Game workspace to be floating even when they have disabled embedded mode:

- I am developing an application and embedded mode is enabled by default.
- I discover that I need to disable embedded mode because I must debug or perform development of my app in its native window mode, rather than embedded mode.
- Even though I must disable embedded mode to debug my app in its native window mode, I want to maintain the same workflow that I previously had with my floating Game workspace:

![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/f23b774c-2d57-42f6-8079-8b35abb658ea)

Because embedded mode is ON by default, I expect that it will not be an issue to allow for an optional empty floatable Game workspace window, just as it is equally not a problem to have any empty not-floating Game workspace. The "Embedding is disabled" text that appears in the Game workspace addresses the usability issue that might lead the user to believe the empty window is unintentional behaviour. If embedded mode was _not_ the default mode, then I would have a different perspective of this.

> Is it due to technical limitations that it cannot be implemented on macOS, or are there other issues?

Directly embedding windows like it is done for X11 and Windows is not possible on macOS.

Eventually it will be supported, but will require a more complex approach (shared IOSurface to display game frame buffer and IPC to route input events from the editor to the game process).

Since we're talking about other platforms, I'll also point out for future reference that this is doable on Wayland too through protocol proxying, like if it were a very stripped down nested microcompositor.

> nd noticed that the embedded viewport is very small - is this intended?

Yes, as integer scaling forces the viewport's scale to be an integer value. Since the window embedding doesn't increase the window size automatically to account for the GUI controls displayed around the game, this "downgrades" the viewport's scale to a lower value.

We could have the window size increase automatically to account for its controls to avoid this issue, but it will require the screen to be large enough to work.

FYI, there's currently an experimental protocol, called `xdg-foreign`, that allows one to export a toplevel from one client and import it in another. Currently it supports setting it as a parent to another toplevel, which seems to be enough for dialog windows. Maybe in the future, a way to embed a surface in another client's surface (as in with subsurfaces) becomes possible.

@dekrain hi! I found a solution that does not require `xdg-foreign` (which as you noted is not enough). This solution consists of a novel (AFAICT) approach: I made a special-purpose super-tiny compositor that "multiplexes" multiple clients into one and remaps all child cleints' toplevels into subsurfaces for the main client on the fly. I run it into a new thread and let everything connect to it.

The reason I made my own compositor is that I could take _a lot_ of shortcuts compared to even hooking up a big compositor library, since we're already working "wayland to wayland". The only thing we care about is basically shell-level surface handling and input redirection (edit: input itself is "free", I mean handling the focus since subsurfaces don't get it automatically) - the rest is passed over to the compositor (with a few ID remaps). This way all features we don't need to touch are basically free (dmabuf, explicit sync, fifo, input method, tablet handling, etc.).

I'll document this approach fully once everything's ready.

I'm currently working on adding a proper control mechanism to let the main client manipulate the embedded fake toplevels.
